iPhone 18 Pro is one of the steps towards achieving Apple's long-term vision of "turning the iPhone into a single piece of glass"—embedding the Face ID module beneath the display.

Making the Face ID array invisible under the screen without compromising display quality in that area has required considerable engineering effort...

Jony Ive once said his long-term design vision for the iPhone was a single slab of glass. Though he has since left the company, this goal has remained unchanged. Apple ultimately wants to embed all components that occupy screen space—including Face ID and the front camera—beneath the display.

The iPhone 18 Pro has taken the first step, but it's far from simple. Face ID requires the TrueDepth module to emit and receive infrared light, yet infrared cannot pass through display pixels.

Apple needed to create gaps between them large enough for infrared to pass through, without producing any visible defects in the display. To achieve this, Apple's engineers designed a different pixel arrangement that increases the spacing between pixels without affecting their display performance.

iFixit used a microscope to reveal this pixel arrangement, and Apple confirmed to me that the overall pixel density across the module has been halved. This could have created another issue: halving pixel density might make that area of the screen noticeably dimmer, so Apple increased the brightness of those pixels to compensate. It also seems to have included a layer that blocks visible light from passing through the gaps, making the component even less conspicuous.

The result is quite remarkable. Basically, no matter how closely you stare at the TrueDepth camera array, you cannot see it. I tried various screen colours and lighting conditions, even with macro photography, and couldn't capture it. This doesn't mean it's completely undetectable—iFixit's microscope images show it clearly—but in everyday use, you would absolutely never notice it.

Currently, this innovation has allowed the Dynamic Island to shrink, enabling support for three Live Activities instead of two. In future iPhone models, the front camera will also be hidden beneath the display. The technology is already technically feasible, but the loss in image quality remains greater than Apple is willing to accept. It's only a matter of time before this is resolved.
